# panelviz

![panelviz logo](reference/figures/logo.svg)

An R package for visualising any panel (longitudinal) data: say which
column is the individual and which is time, and get publication-ready
charts.

## Overview

panelviz is an R package for visualising any panel (longitudinal) data.
Given the column that identifies the individual and the column that
records time, it recognises the time format, aggregates the data over
time and across individuals, and draws publication-ready charts. It
provides a consistent set of functions for each stage:

- [`read_panel()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/read_panel.md),
  [`as_panel()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/as_panel.md)
  and
  [`as_panel_wide()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/as_panel_wide.md)
  declare a data frame, file or URL as a panel (csv, tsv, Stata, SPSS,
  rds).
- [`panel_aggregate()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_aggregate.md)
  aggregates in two stages: within each individual over time, then
  across individuals by group.
- [`panel_line()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_line.md),
  [`panel_heatmap()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_heatmap.md),
  [`panel_spaghetti()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_spaghetti.md),
  [`panel_tracking()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_tracking.md),
  [`panel_band()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_band.md),
  [`panel_bar()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_bar.md),
  [`panel_stacked()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_stacked.md)
  and
  [`panel_distribution()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_distribution.md)
  draw the data. All share the same arguments.
- [`panel_figure()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_figure.md)
  and
  [`save_panel()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/save_panel.md)
  compose numbered multi-panel figures and save any chart.
- [`panel_styles()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_styles.md)
  and
  [`use_panel_style()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/use_panel_style.md)
  select one of five looks: `economist` (the default), `ft`, `clean`,
  `dark` and `mono`.

``` r

library(panelviz)
nls <- read_panel("https://www.stata-press.com/data/r18/nlswork.dta", id = idcode, time = year)

nls
#> # A tidy panel: 4,711 individuals x 15 periods (year), 1968-01-01 to 1988-01-01
#> # id = idcode | time = year | unbalanced (40% of id-period cells filled) | 28,534 obs

panel_line(nls, "ln_wage", by = "race")
```

![Line chart of log wage by race](reference/figures/nlswork_line.png)

## Why

Panel data consists of repeated observations of the same individuals
over time, stored in long format with one row per individual and time
point. It arises in economics and business (firms, households, markets),
public health and epidemiology (patients, clinic visits, countries),
education and psychology (pupils, terms, study sessions), tourism and
retail (regions, stores, quarters) and organisational analytics
(employees, weeks). Terminology differs by discipline: *panel data* in
economics, *longitudinal data* or *repeated measures* in medicine and
psychology, *time-series cross-section* in political science, and
*grouped* or *hierarchical time series* in forecasting. The individual
may be called a subject, unit, entity or participant, and time a wave,
occasion, visit or period.

Analysing such data involves a recurring sequence of steps: identifying
the individual and time variables and parsing the time format,
aggregating over time within each individual, aggregating across
individuals into groups, and presenting the result in a form suitable
for publication. Errors tend to arise at the aggregation steps, for
example summing a stock variable where its last value is meant, or
reporting a statistic for a group too small to be meaningful.

panelviz implements this sequence behind a single declaration of the
individual and time variables. It originates in the plotting functions
of [`wpa`](https://github.com/microsoft/wpa) and
[`vivainsights`](https://github.com/microsoft/vivainsights), which were
developed for weekly Viva Insights person-level data, and generalises
them to any panel.

## How

- **Time formats are detected.** Dates, hourly timestamps, years,
  two-digit years, `"1998 Q1"`, `"2020-03"`, ISO weeks, `yyyymm`, text
  dates, Stata `%tm`, `%tq` and `%ty` values and plain indices are
  supported. Ambiguous dates and repeated id-time rows stop with an
  informative error instead of being guessed.
- **Aggregation has two stages, because a panel has two dimensions.**
  Time is collapsed within each individual first (`fun_time`: `sum` for
  flows, `last` for stocks), then individuals are collapsed into groups
  (`fun_group`: `mean`, `median`, `p90` or any function). `min_n`
  suppresses groups with too few individuals, and the chart footer
  reports it.
- **Every chart takes the same arguments.** `by`, `period`, `fun_time`,
  `fun_group`, `min_n`, `tag`, `source`, `style` and `return = "table"`
  have the same meaning in each function.
- **Text is derived from the data.** The title reports what changed,
  which group leads or which overtook another; the subtitle states what
  was calculated; Stata variable labels are used as names. Both can be
  overridden with `title` and `subtitle`.
- **Axes select their own units** (`950`, `1.2K`, `6M`), detect
  percentages, and show the year only where it changes.
- **Fonts degrade gracefully.** The best available condensed typeface is
  used
  ([`panel_font()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_font.md));
  a device that cannot render it redraws with its default font.

## Tested on

| Dataset | Individual and time |
|----|----|
| Stata `nlswork` | numeric id, two-digit years, unbalanced |
| Stata `grunfeld`, `abdata` | company or firm id, year |
| Stata `reshape1` | wide: `inc80 inc81 ...`, `ue80 ue81 ...` |
| `Gasoline`, `Fatalities` (Rdatasets) | country or state id, year |
| `tourism` (Rdatasets) | composite id of region, state and purpose; `1998 Q1` quarters |
| Gapminder | country, 5-year steps |
| COVID-19 daily counts | 198 countries, ISO dates, 816 days |
| `wpa` sample data | hashed person id, text dates `12/15/2019` |

`data-raw/fetch.R` and `data-raw/check_examples.R` reproduce these
checks.

## Installation

``` r

# The development version from GitHub:
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("AdvancedPeopleAnalytics/panelviz")

# or
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("AdvancedPeopleAnalytics/panelviz")
```

panelviz requires R 4.1 or later. The optional packages `haven` (Stata
and SPSS files), `readr` (csv), `systemfonts` and `ragg` (typefaces and
font rendering) extend what it can read and how it renders.

After installing, run
[`vignette("getting-started", "panelviz")`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/articles/getting-started.md)
for a worked introduction: declare the panel, aggregate in two stages,
and draw each chart type on simulated data.

## Use with Claude Code

The repository ships a [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
skill, `.claude/skills/panelviz/SKILL.md`, that lets Claude use panelviz
as a charting engine: point it at a file, name the individual and time
columns, and it writes and checks the chart. Open Claude Code in a clone
of this repository and it is picked up automatically. To use it in any
project, copy the folder to `~/.claude/skills/panelviz/`.

## Examples

Every command below is the one that produced the output next to it.
First, the data:

``` r

library(panelviz)

# Stata dta, text csv and daily csv, straight from the web: id = who, time = when
nls   <- read_panel("https://www.stata-press.com/data/r18/nlswork.dta",
                    id = idcode, time = year, source = "US Bureau of Labor Statistics, NLS of Young Women")
gm    <- read_panel("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plotly/datasets/master/gapminderDataFiveYear.csv",
                    id = country, time = year, source = "Gapminder")
tour  <- read_panel("https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/tsibble/tourism.csv",
                    id = c(Region, State, Purpose), time = Quarter, source = "Tourism Research Australia")
covid <- read_panel("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datasets/covid-19/main/data/countries-aggregated.csv",
                    id = Country, time = Date, source = "Johns Hopkins CSSE")
gf    <- read_panel("https://www.stata-press.com/data/r18/grunfeld.dta",
                    id = company, time = year, source = "Grunfeld (1958)")
```

### Declare the panel

Say which column is the individual and which is time. panelviz
recognises the time format, sorts the data and reports its shape: 4,711
women observed in 15 survey years, unbalanced because not everyone
answered every year.

- `id`: one column, or several for a composite key
  (`c(Region, State, Purpose)`)
- `time`: the time column, in almost any format
- `source`: printed as “Source: …” in every chart footer

``` r

print(nls, n = 3)
```

    # A tidy panel: 4,711 individuals x 15 periods (year), 1968-01-01 to 1988-01-01
    # id = idcode | time = year | unbalanced (40% of id-period cells filled) | 28,534 obs
    # A tibble: 28,534 × 23

    1 1     1970-01-01      1    70       51    18 2 [Blac…     0       1    12        0        0      1
    2 1     1971-01-01      1    71       51    19 2 [Blac…     1       0    12        0        0      1

    #   ttl_exp <dbl>, tenure <dbl>, hours <dbl>, wks_work <dbl>, ln_wage <dbl>

### Time formats are detected

The same call handles quarters, ISO weeks, US-style dates, `yyyymm`
numbers and hourly timestamps. Ambiguous input (`01/02/2020`) stops with
a message instead of guessing; pass `time_format` to choose.

- `time_format`: `NULL` (detect), a
  [`strptime()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/strptime.html) string such as
  `"%d.%m.%Y"`, or `"year"`, `"quarter"`, `"month"`, `"week"`, `"index"`

``` r

what <- list(quarters = c("1998 Q1", "1998 Q2"), iso_weeks = c("2020-W01", "2020-W02"),
             us_dates = c("12/15/2019", "12/22/2019"), yyyymm = c(202001, 202002),
             hourly = c("2024-03-01 00:00:00", "2024-03-01 01:00:00"), two_digit_years = c(68, 69))
sapply(what, function(x) unlist(panel_meta(as_panel(data.frame(id = 1, t = x), id, t))[c("kind", "freq")]))
```

         quarters  iso_weeks us_dates yyyymm  hourly two_digit_years
    kind "quarter" "week"    "date"   "month" "hour" "year"
    freq "quarter" "week"    "week"   "month" "hour" "year"         

### Wide data

One column per period (and per measure) is pivoted to long format first.
Here Stata’s `reshape1` has `inc80 inc81 inc82` and `ue80 ue81 ue82`.

- `cols`: the period columns (tidyselect)
- `names_pattern`: regular expression with two groups, measure then
  period; `NULL` when the column names are the periods

``` r

wide <- as_panel_wide(haven::read_dta("https://www.stata-press.com/data/r18/reshape1.dta"),
                       id, cols = c(starts_with("inc"), starts_with("ue")),
                       names_pattern = "^(inc|ue)(\\d+)$")
wide
```

    # A tidy panel: 3 individuals x 3 periods (year), 1980-01-01 to 1982-01-01
    # id = id | time = period | balanced | 9 obs
    # A tibble: 9 × 7
      .id   .time         id   sex period   inc    ue
    * <chr> <date>     <dbl> <dbl> <chr>  <dbl> <dbl>
    1 1     1980-01-01     1     0 80      5000     0
    2 1     1981-01-01     1     0 81      5500     1
    3 1     1982-01-01     1     0 82      6000     0
    4 2     1980-01-01     2     1 80      2000     1
    5 2     1981-01-01     2     1 81      2200     0
    6 2     1982-01-01     2     1 82      3300     0
    7 3     1980-01-01     3     0 80      3000     0
    8 3     1981-01-01     3     0 81      2000     0
    9 3     1982-01-01     3     0 82      1000     1

### Aggregate in two stages

Panel data has two dimensions, so aggregation has two stages. First,
within each individual, time is collapsed into `period` (`fun_time`).
Then individuals are collapsed into groups (`fun_group`). Here: each
tourism flow’s yearly *total* trips, then the *mean* across flows in
each state. `.n` is the number of individuals behind each value.

- `vars`: numeric columns to summarise (default all)
- `by`: grouping column(s); `NULL` for one overall series; `".id"` keeps
  individuals
- `period`: `"hour"`, `"day"`, `"week"`, `"month"`, `"quarter"`,
  `"year"` or `"all"`
- `fun_time`, `fun_group`:
  `mean median sum sd min max first last n share p10 p90 ...` or any
  function
- `min_n`: drop group-periods with fewer individuals

``` r

panel_aggregate(tour, "Trips", by = "State", period = "year", fun_time = "sum", fun_group = "mean")
```

    # A tibble: 160 × 4
       .period    State Trips    .n
       <date>     <chr> <dbl> <int>
     1 1998-01-01 ACT    463.     4
     2 1999-01-01 ACT    495.     4
     3 2000-01-01 ACT    523.     4
     4 2001-01-01 ACT    522.     4
     5 2002-01-01 ACT    493.     4
     6 2003-01-01 ACT    486.     4
     7 2004-01-01 ACT    470.     4
     8 2005-01-01 ACT    497.     4
     9 2006-01-01 ACT    473.     4
    10 2007-01-01 ACT    489.     4
    # ℹ 150 more rows

### Line: one overall series

The title is computed from the data. Axes use the best units, and the
year appears only where it changes.

- `var`: the variable to plot

``` r

panel_line(nls, "ln_wage")
```

![Line: one overall series](reference/figures/ex_line.png)

### Line: one line per group

Lines are labelled directly. When the leader changes, the headline says
who overtook whom.

- `by`: the grouping column
- `max_groups`: keep the largest groups (default 10)

``` r

panel_line(gm, "lifeExp", by = "continent")
```

![Line: one line per group](reference/figures/ex_line_by.png)

### Line: highlight one group, index to 100

Grey out every group except the one being discussed, and rebase every
group so that its first period equals 100.

- `highlight`: group name(s) to emphasise
- `index`: `TRUE` rebases each group to 100 at its first period

``` r

panel_line(gf, "invest", by = "company", highlight = "1", index = TRUE)
```

![Line: highlight one group, index to
100](reference/figures/ex_line_highlight.png)

### Coarsen time: quarters to years

`period` changes the time unit, and `fun_time` says how each
individual’s quarters combine: here the yearly total of each tourism
flow, averaged by state.

- `period = "year"`
- `fun_time = "sum"`: flows add up; use `"last"` for stocks and
  cumulative counts

``` r

panel_line(tour, "Trips", by = "State", period = "year", fun_time = "sum")
```

![Coarsen time: quarters to years](reference/figures/ex_line_period.png)

### A different summary, and a privacy floor

Show the 90th percentile instead of the mean, and hide any state-year
with fewer than 30 individuals. The footer says groups were hidden.

- `fun_group = "p90"`
- `min_n = 30`

``` r

panel_line(tour, "Trips", by = "State", period = "year", fun_group = "p90", min_n = 30)
```

![A different summary, and a privacy
floor](reference/figures/ex_line_p90.png)

### Small multiples and a log scale

One panel per group with free y axes; `log = TRUE` is useful when groups
differ by orders of magnitude.

- `facet = TRUE`
- `log = TRUE`

``` r

panel_line(gm, "gdpPercap", by = "continent", facet = TRUE, log = TRUE)
```

![Small multiples and a log scale](reference/figures/ex_line_facet.png)

### Heatmap: groups by time

Rows are groups, columns are periods, colour is the value. Rows are
sorted by level. With `by = NULL` the rows are individuals.

- `by`, `period`, `fun_time`, `fun_group` as above
- `max_rows`: rows shown when rows are individuals (default 40)

``` r

panel_heatmap(tour, "Trips", by = "State", period = "year")
```

![Heatmap: groups by time](reference/figures/ex_heat.png)

### Heatmap of individuals, diverging colours

With `by = NULL` every row is one individual (here 30 of 142 countries,
evenly spaced by level). `diverge` centres the colour scale on the
overall mean, so blue is below average and red above.

- `by = NULL`: rows are individuals
- `max_rows`: how many rows to show
- `diverge = TRUE`

``` r

panel_heatmap(gm, "lifeExp", max_rows = 30, diverge = TRUE)
```

![Heatmap of individuals, diverging
colours](reference/figures/ex_heat_div.png)

### Spaghetti: individuals and the average

Thin lines are individuals, the bold line is the group summary. A log
axis keeps small firms visible next to large ones.

- `n_ids`: how many individual lines to draw (random sample,
  reproducible with `seed`)
- `log = TRUE`

``` r

panel_spaghetti(gf, "invest", log = TRUE)
```

![Spaghetti: individuals and the average](reference/figures/ex_spag.png)

### Tracking: a series and its rolling average

Cumulative counts per country become a weekly series: each country’s
last value of the week, summed across countries, with a 4-week rolling
average.

- `window`: periods in the rolling average
- `fun_time = "last"`, `fun_group = "sum"`

``` r

panel_tracking(covid, "Confirmed", period = "week", fun_time = "last", fun_group = "sum", window = 4)
```

![Tracking: a series and its rolling
average](reference/figures/ex_tracking.png)

### Band: the spread across individuals

The median line with a shaded percentile band shows spread, not just the
centre. The headline reports whether the spread widened.

- `lower`, `upper`: band edges (`"p10"`, `"p90"`, …)
- `centre`: line summary (default `"median"`)

``` r

panel_band(nls, "ln_wage", by = "race", lower = "p10", upper = "p90")
```

![Band: the spread across individuals](reference/figures/ex_band.png)

### Bars: ranked groups

Time is collapsed (`period = "all"`). Names sit inside long bars; group
sizes are in the subtitle.

- `top_n`: groups shown (default 15)
- `decreasing`: sort order

``` r

panel_bar(tour, "Trips", by = "State")
```

![Bars: ranked groups](reference/figures/ex_bar.png)

### Stacked bars: composition

Several measures stacked within each group. Segment labels that would
not fit are hidden.

- `vars`: two or more columns
- `min_label`: smallest share of the longest bar that gets a label

``` r

panel_stacked(gf, c("invest", "kstock"), by = "company", top_n = 6)
```

![Stacked bars: composition](reference/figures/ex_stacked.png)

### Distribution of individuals

Each individual’s average over time, then the distribution across
individuals, by group.

- `period = "all"`, `fun_time = "mean"`

``` r

panel_distribution(nls, "ln_wage", by = "race")
```

![Distribution of individuals](reference/figures/ex_dist.png)

### Style, tag, title and source

Five looks ship with the package: `economist` (default), `ft`, `clean`,
`dark`, `mono`. Any computed text can be overridden. The numbered square
is for figure references.

- `style`: one of
  [`panel_styles()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_styles.md)
  (or `use_panel_style("ft")` for the session)
- `tag`: number or label in the top-right square
- `title`, `subtitle`, `source`

``` r

panel_bar(tour, "Trips", by = "State", style = "ft", tag = 2,
          title = "New South Wales and Victoria dominate", source = "Tourism Research Australia, 1998-2017")
```

![Style, tag, title and source](reference/figures/ex_style.png)

### Numbered figure from several charts

[`panel_figure()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_figure.md)
lays charts out under one headline, numbers the panels and shares one
source and notes footer.

- `ncol`, `heights`, `widths`: layout
- `title`, `subtitle`, `source`, `notes`: shared text
- `tags = TRUE`: number the panels

``` r

fig <- panel_figure(
  list(panel_line(gm, "lifeExp", by = "continent"),
       panel_bar(tour, "Trips", by = "State"),
       panel_band(nls, "ln_wage", by = "race", lower = "p10", upper = "p90"),
       panel_heatmap(tour, "Trips", by = "Purpose")),
  title = "Four views, one grammar", subtitle = "The same panelviz calls on three different panels",
  source = "Gapminder; Tourism Research Australia; US Bureau of Labor Statistics",
  notes = "Individuals are countries, tourism flows and women respectively.")
save_panel(fig, "figure.png", width = 14, height = 9)
```

![Numbered figure from several charts](reference/figures/ex_figure.png)

### Get the numbers behind any chart

Every chart takes `return = "table"` and hands back exactly what it
drew.

- `return = "table"`

``` r

panel_line(gm, "lifeExp", by = "continent", return = "table")
```

    # A tibble: 60 × 5
       .period    continent lifeExp    .n .group
       <date>     <chr>       <dbl> <int> <chr>
     1 1952-01-01 Africa       39.1    52 Africa
     2 1957-01-01 Africa       41.3    52 Africa
     3 1962-01-01 Africa       43.3    52 Africa
     4 1967-01-01 Africa       45.3    52 Africa
     5 1972-01-01 Africa       47.5    52 Africa
     6 1977-01-01 Africa       49.6    52 Africa
     7 1982-01-01 Africa       51.6    52 Africa
     8 1987-01-01 Africa       53.3    52 Africa
     9 1992-01-01 Africa       53.6    52 Africa
    10 1997-01-01 Africa       53.6    52 Africa
    # ℹ 50 more rows

> **Not to be confused with
> [panelView](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=panelView)** on CRAN,
> which plots treatment status and outcomes for causal-inference panels.
> panelviz is a general toolkit: import, aggregate and chart any panel.

## Known issues

1.  Not on CRAN yet.
2.  Stata `%tw` weeks are read approximately.
3.  Wide data with several measures needs a `names_pattern`; there is no
    automatic guess.
4.  The red tag and numbered squares are drawn when a chart is printed
    or saved, so they are lost if a chart is placed inside patchwork or
    cowplot; use
    [`panel_figure()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_figure.md)
    instead.
5.  Group names in direct line labels can still overlap when many series
    end at nearly the same value.
6.  Only R for now.

## Authors

panelviz is written by Carlos Morales and [Martin
Chan](https://github.com/martinctc). It generalises the plotting
approach of [`wpa`](https://github.com/microsoft/wpa) and
[`vivainsights`](https://github.com/microsoft/vivainsights), which the
two authors developed at Microsoft.

## Licence

MIT. Generalises the plotting approach of `wpa` and `vivainsights`
(Microsoft, MIT).

# Package index

## Declare and import panels

Say which column is the individual and which is time, or read a file or
URL straight into a panel.

- [`as_panel()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/as_panel.md)
  : Declare a data frame as a panel
- [`as_panel_wide()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/as_panel_wide.md)
  : Declare a wide-format data frame as a panel
- [`read_panel()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/read_panel.md)
  : Read a panel from a file or URL
- [`panel_meta()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_meta.md)
  : Panel structure metadata

## Aggregate

Aggregate within individuals over time, then across individuals by
group, with an optional group-size floor.

- [`panel_aggregate()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_aggregate.md)
  : Aggregate a panel over time and across individuals

## Charts

One chart per question. All chart functions share the same arguments for
selecting groups, periods, aggregation and style.

- [`panel_plot()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_plot.md)
  : Plot a panel with a chosen chart type
- [`panel_line()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_line.md)
  : Line chart of a panel variable over time
- [`panel_heatmap()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_heatmap.md)
  : Heatmap of groups (rows) by time (columns)
- [`panel_spaghetti()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_spaghetti.md)
  : Individual trajectories with the group average on top
- [`panel_tracking()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_tracking.md)
  : Tracking chart: the period average with a rolling average
- [`panel_band()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_band.md)
  : Median with an inter-quantile band across individuals
- [`panel_bar()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_bar.md)
  : Ranked bars of groups
- [`panel_stacked()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_stacked.md)
  : Stacked bars: how several measures add up within each group
- [`panel_distribution()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_distribution.md)
  : Distribution of individuals

## Compose and save

- [`panel_figure()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_figure.md)
  : Compose several charts into one numbered figure
- [`save_panel()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/save_panel.md)
  : Save a chart or figure

## Style

Five looks, set globally or per chart, plus the theme and font hooks
behind them.

- [`panel_styles()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_styles.md)
  : Available looks
- [`use_panel_style()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/use_panel_style.md)
  : Set the look for the session
- [`theme_panel()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/theme_panel.md)
  : Theme for panel graphics
- [`panel_font()`](https://advancedpeopleanalytics.github.io/panelviz/reference/panel_font.md)
  : Best available condensed font
